Measuring a Reliable Reader

A reliable reader must distinguish fetching from understanding what arrived. A successful transport can still deliver a consent wall, a challenge form, or a fragment that ends before the argument does. Treating an HTTP status as proof of content turns an ordinary infrastructure signal into a dangerous semantic claim.

The safer design keeps the original representation, the extracted prose, and the verification evidence separate. Each layer answers a different question. The fetcher says what the server returned, the extractor finds likely main content, and the verifier asks whether independent facts support calling that content complete.

Independent evidence

Headings are useful because they form a compact manifest already present in the document. If the visible article contains sections about methods, results, limitations, and conclusions, an extraction missing the final two headings is plainly suspect even when the surviving paragraphs read smoothly.

Length is another signal when its reference is external to extraction. A publisher supplied word count, an API item manifest, or the visible main DOM can reveal a large gap.
